summary:
UrbanAstro is a scientific mission-planning and public outreach web application designed to evaluate landing site viability at the lunar south pole (latitudes ≤ -80°S). Combining high-precision JPL SPICE planetary ephemerides (DE421, MOON_ME_DE421) with real Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LOLA) Digital Elevation Models (240 m/px), our FastAPI backend performs 360-azimuth curvature-corrected horizon raycasting over a 100 km radius and native-resolution touchdown slope estimation.

It directly addresses the challenge of polar surface operations—where grazing solar angles, steep crater walls, and lunar librations create rapid transitions between permanent shadow and continuous sunlight—by automating a three-gate GO / NO-GO mission feasibility engine alongside interactive Three.js 3D terrain simulations and synchronized Plotly telemetry charts. By offering both a rigorous Engineer Mode for mission planners and an accessible Explorer Mode for students and the public, UrbanAstro bridges open-science lunar datasets with actionable landing decisions for future Artemis and CLPS polar missions.
details:
What It Does & How It Works

UrbanAstro is a web tool that helps mission planners and students check if a landing site at the lunar south pole is safe and viable. When you pick a target site (like Shackleton Crater Rim, Connecting Ridge, or Cabeus Crater) or type in custom coordinates and a launch date, our Python backend runs three steps:

1. Sun & Earth Tracking: Using Skyfield and real NASA JPL SPICE files (de421.bsp and moon_pa_de421_1900-2050.bpc), it calculates the exact angles of the Sun and Earth from the lunar surface over time, accounting for the Sun's width (0.265°) and lunar librations.

2. 360° Terrain Shadow Check: For sites at or below -80°S, our code reads elevation data derived from NASA's high-resolution LRO/LOLA South Polar DEM (LDEM_80S_40MPP_ADJ.TIF, locally resampled to 240 m/px as LDEM_80S_240MPP_COMPACT.TIF for low-latency cloud execution) and shoots 360 rays out to 100 km around the lander.

3. Slope & Power Verdict: It measures the ground slope across a 1.2 km landing zone using a 5x5 pixel grid, calculates how long the Sun and Earth stay visible without interruption, compares vertical vs. horizontal solar panels, and outputs a clear GO, NO-GO, or INCONCLUSIVE decision.

Why It Matters

At the lunar south pole, the Sun stays very low on the horizon (usually under 6°), which means crater rims cast huge shadows for days at a time. Moving a lander by just a few kilometers—from a Permanently Shadowed Region (0% sun) or the steep inner wall of Shackleton Crater (21.5° slope) onto Connecting Ridge—shifts the verdict from NO-GO to nearly 100% illumination (GO).

How We Built It (Tools & Stack)

- Backend: Python 3, FastAPI, Uvicorn, Skyfield, Rasterio, NumPy, and SciPy.

- Frontend & 3D Views: HTML, CSS, JavaScript, React 18, Three.js (for the 3D terrain mesh, live shadows, DTE signal beam, 3D lunar globe, and Earth-to-Moon transfer view), and Plotly.js (for interactive timeline charts and the 360° polar skyplot).

- Data Sources: NASA/JPL NAIF SPICE kernels and NASA PDS LRO/LOLA South Polar Digital Elevation Models.

- Repository & Technical Paper: Full source code, our 1-click setup script (backend_loader.py), and our technical report are available at https://github.com/thuliobandeira402/Nasa-Space-Apps

Key Decisions Our Team Made

- Two Modes in One App: We noticed specialists want raw data while students just want to understand what is happening. So we built an instant switch between Engineer Mode (custom coordinates, time steps, telemetry gates, and scenario comparison) and Explorer Mode (simple explanations and visual highlights).

- No Fake Terrain: Outside the -80°S polar map coverage, our app does not invent fake 3D hills. Instead, it switches to a clean reference sphere and marks the slope check as INCONCLUSIVE so it never gives a false "GO".

- Real Mission Windows: Instead of just looking at monthly averages, our GO/NO-GO rules check for continuous sunlit stretches (at least 156 hours) and continuous Earth radio windows (at least 72 hours) so a lander can actually survive and send data back home.
